nameStory: This plant gets its "foxglove" name from its tubular flowers that resemble the fingers of a glove, just like the more familiar European foxgloves. The "South African" part tells us exactly where this beauty originally calls home - the warm regions of southern Africa, far from New England's chilly winters.
description: South African foxglove is a tender annual plant with striking tubular flowers that bloom in warm weather. It typically grows 2-4 feet tall with soft, heart-shaped leaves and produces distinctive horn-shaped seed capsules after flowering. This is definitely not a native New Englander - it's a tropical visitor that occasionally shows up in gardens or as an escaped ornamental, explaining why it's been spotted only once in our region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers with five petals that flare out at the mouth, usually pink, purple, or white with darker markings inside that guide pollinators

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, velvety heart-shaped leaves that feel fuzzy to the touch and are arranged alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Very distinctive horned seed capsules that split into two curved, pointed sections resembling devil's horns when mature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant reaching 2-4 feet tall with branching stems that feel slightly sticky when touched

habitat: In New England, this would only survive as a garden annual or in very protected, warm microclimates during summer. If found wild, it would likely be near areas where seeds escaped from cultivation, such as around compost piles, garden borders, or disturbed soil near homes where it was previously grown.

seasonality.spring: Seeds would need to be planted after all danger of frost has passed, as this tropical plant cannot tolerate cold temperatures.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and blooming season, when the tubular flowers appear and the plant reaches full size in warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing seeds, but the plant will die with the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors - any seeds would need greenhouse protection to survive until spring planting.

funFact: The genus name Ceratotheca literally means "horn capsule" in Greek, perfectly describing those wild-looking curved seed pods that split open like tiny devil horns - making this one of the few plants whose scientific name actually helps you remember what to look for!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with common foxglove (Digitalis), but South African foxglove has heart-shaped fuzzy leaves instead of lance-shaped smooth ones, and those distinctive horned seed capsules are a dead giveaway - no true foxglove makes anything like them.
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the "foxglove" common name, this plant is in the sesame family (Pedaliaceae), not the plantain family like true foxgloves. This means they're not closely related at all - they just happen to have similarly shaped tubular flowers that reminded people of glove fingers.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus found in New England, South African foxglove is most similar to other members of the sesame family. However, most of its relatives are tropical plants rarely encountered here, making those distinctive horned seed capsules and fuzzy heart-shaped leaves your best identification features compared to any other flowering plant in the region.
